city.caveat: This is the official city record as kept, without adjustments. It joins several observing sites over the years, and a move, a new instrument or the city growing around a station can shift readings (city growth mostly warms nights); NOAA's adjusted climate datasets correct for these. Treat any single number as approximate.

text.t_yest: November 13: a typical high, but a warm night
text.p_yest: The high of 71°F was typical for November 13. The normal high for the date is 71°F, and the record is 89°F (1949). The low of 60°F was the 8th warmest November 13 low (tied) of 153 since 1874.
text.t_rec: Record highs keep coming. Record lows have nearly stopped.
text.p_rec: If San Diego's climate weren't changing, every year would have the same chance of holding a daily record. Since 2000, San Diego has set 3 standing record lows, far fewer than the 64 that chance alone would give, and 98 record highs, far more than the 64 that chance alone would give. The 1950s hold the most record highs of any decade (47). San Diego's all-time high is 111°F, on September 26, 1963.
text.t_chg: San Diego has warmed, days and nights alike
text.p_chg: Across 151 complete years: San Diego's average low has risen +0.35°F per decade (95% range +0.30 to +0.40), about +5.2°F since 1875. San Diego's average high has risen +0.29°F per decade (95% range +0.23 to +0.34), about +4.3°F since 1875.
text.t_mon: Lows rose in all 12 months. Highs rose in all 12 months.
text.p_rain: San Diego's yearly precipitation shows no clear long-term change (−0.01 inches per decade, a range that includes zero). The 1991–2020 normal is 9.8 inches a year. The wettest year was 1884 (27.59 in); the driest, 1953 (3.41 in). San Diego almost never sees snow (the 1991–2020 average is 0.0 inches a winter), so there's no snowfall chart.
